Tomaszow Mazowiecki Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Tomaszów Mazowiecki, Poland

Not demolished. Tomaszów, founded in 1830, saw Jewish settlement from the turn of the 19th century, with a kehilla established in 1831 on land granted by Duke Antoni Ostrowski (before which residents buried their dead in Inowłódz); kehilla leader Dawid Halpern fenced the grounds and organized a burial society under Rabbi Lejke Zilber. By 1921, 10,070 Jews (36%) grew to 13,000 by 1939. A December 1940 ghetto held 16,500 people from Tomaszów and elsewhere (Łódź, Płock, Warsaw); some were sent to labor camps at Bliżyn, Skarżysko-Kamienna, and Pionek in 1941, while around 15,000 were deported to Treblinka that year, with remaining residents transported to Starachowice in 1943. This cemetery held numerous execution victims during the war, including 21 people killed in the March 21, 1943 'Operation Purim'; a 2002 reburial added remains of dozens more, killed by Polish residents near Lubochnia in January 1943. Notable burials include January Uprising veterans, Bund activist Abram Jakubowicz, poet Henryk Kamiński, and Rabbi Jakub Eliasz Wieliczkier, leader of the town's religious court. The last burial occurred in 1983 (Stanisław Talman); a 1947 memorial marks the ghetto's 15,000 Treblinka victims, alongside a separate memorial to the 'Operation Purim' dead. Beniamin Yaari-Wald led a full tombstone inventory (1995-1999), published as a book in Israel.
